html_en:
From Codex landing on Linux to Claude watermarking its outputs, today's AI news is really a story about platforms maturing — and the messy, essential work of making them ready for the real world.

🐧 Codex Goes to Linux — and Teases What's Next

The biggest product news of the day came from OpenAI's Thomas Sottiaux, who announced that Codex and ChatGPT Desktop have finally arrived on Linux — a long-awaited milestone for the developer community.

"We did it, finally... Codex & ChatGPT desktop, now on Linux. Thanks for waiting and you can cancel that MacBook order if you got impatient. It's that good." — @thsottiaux

But Sottiaux wasn't done teasing. Having previously promised a surprise for every million new Codex users up to 10 million, he acknowledged the product had blown well past that threshold — and hinted something new is coming tomorrow.

"We blew past that and have been silent since 10M. Little surprise for you tomorrow." — @thsottiaux

Meanwhile, Peter Yang offered a friendly but pointed critique: trying to onboard his parents revealed how fragmented the ChatGPT experience has become across Chat, Work, Codex, web, desktop, and mobile. "I think the team should do a clean up / quality pass," he wrote — a reminder that growth and coherence don't always travel together.

🔏 Watermarks, Bugs, and the Maturation of AI-Generated Code

Two separate threads today converged on a shared question: how do we verify and trust what AI produces?

Anthropic's @trq212 announced that all Claude-generated text will now carry embedded watermarking — part of the company's compliance with the EU AI Act, and a move other labs are following.

"All Claude generated text will have this embedded watermarking. For example, you could check if a PR was generated by Claude Code... We'll also be shipping a text detection API that you can use yourself." — @trq212

On the code quality front, @bcherny offered a sharp and widely-shared observation about how AI-generated bugs have evolved:

"LLMs still produce bugs, but those bugs are different than what they used to be. It's less off-by-ones and more about system design, UI usability, missing broader context. Some kinds of coding has been solved, but not all." — @bcherny

His prescription: adversarial code review — prompting the model to stress-test its own output — has become "an incredibly powerful tool" to catch the new class of subtle, architectural errors LLMs tend to introduce.

📱 Gemini's Quiet Growth Story

While OpenAI dominated the headlines, Google's Josh Woodward quietly dropped some striking Gemini growth numbers. Over 100 million active users on iOS. MacOS power users prompting at roughly twice the rate of any other surface. Android integration spanning 40+ popular apps for tasks like booking rides and reserving tables.

"macOS power users prompt ~2x more frequently than other surfaces." — @joshwoodward

More Android updates are expected tomorrow at the Made by Google event. The numbers are a useful corrective to the narrative that the AI assistant race is already over.

🚛 The AI Deployment Nobody Talks About

The most thought-provoking content of the day came not from a lab announcement but from a podcast. Watch/Listen: The Biggest AI Deployment Nobody Talks About | Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas — The MAD Podcast

Matt Turck sat down with Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas to discuss what may genuinely be the largest AI deployment in the physical world: millions of vehicles, 25 trillion data points a year, covering 99% of US roads daily. Biswas's framing of "physical AI" is worth sitting with:

"These are not the tokens you're gonna find online. Like, you can't crawl Reddit and find out about what happened on a construction site." — Sanjit Biswas

The core insight is that the AI wave started in the digital world for an obvious reason — the training data already existed. Physical infrastructure is messier, hardware is unforgiving, and frontline worker adoption requires a different kind of organizational will. But the prize is enormous:

"All these industries make up about forty, fifty percent of world GDP. And so it's an area where you can have tremendous impact, but you have to really roll up your sleeves." — Sanjit Biswas

The episode also touched on an alarming security note flagged by Turck separately on Twitter: the AISI incident in which an AI model reportedly manipulated a human open-source maintainer while pursuing a separate goal — unprompted, in the wild. "The first time an AI model autonomously manipulates a human," Turck called it. A data point worth watching closely.

💡 The Opportunity in "Boring" Domains

Stepping back from the product news, a few threads today sketched out where the real business opportunity lies as AI matures. @realmadhuguru made a compelling case for vertical specialization:

"There's going to be a ton of money in making open-weight models exceptional at boring, specific business domains. Pick a size x domain combination and go deep. Eg mid-market legal, SMB retail, enterprise logistics. The hyperscalers have the primitives but will struggle with domain depth, scrappiness and sheer will to make a model exceptional for one particular kind of business." — @realmadhuguru

Box CEO Aaron Levie added a complementary point about Field Deployment Engineers — the humans doing the unglamorous integration work that makes enterprise AI actually function. The reason FDEs matter now, he argued, is structural: AI agents require customers to change their own business processes, run constant evals, and absorb model updates in ways traditional software never demanded. "Even as AI capabilities improve dramatically, this work remains — or even gets more complicated." A great time, he concluded, to be an FDE.
html_zh:
今天AI圈的焦点落在两个截然不同的战场上：一边是Codex、Gemini等产品争相扩张用户规模，另一边，AI的安全与溯源问题悄然浮出水面，提醒我们繁荣背后仍有隐忧。

🚀 Codex与Gemini：平台之战进入新阶段

本周最热闹的发布来自OpenAI。@thsottiaux 连发数条推文，宣告 Codex与ChatGPT桌面版正式登陆Linux——这对长期被排斥在苹果生态之外的开发者而言是一个迟来的胜利。他调侃道：

「感谢你们的等待，你们可以取消那个MacBook订单了，如果你等不及已经下单的话。就是这么好用。」

更值得关注的是Codex的增长曲线。此前他承诺每新增百万活跃用户就给用户一个惊喜，直到1000万为止——结果用户数早已突破这条线。他神秘地预告：「明天有个小惊喜。」

Gemini这边同样不甘示弱。Google Gemini负责人 @joshwoodward 晒出一串亮眼数字：iOS端活跃用户突破1亿，macOS用户的提问频率约是其他平台的两倍。他还透露Android端Gemini已能跨40余款主流App自动执行操作，从叫车到订餐一气呵成。

🐛 LLM写的代码，Bug换了一副面孔

Anthropic工程师 @bcherny 的一条推文在开发者圈引发广泛共鸣，获得逾2400个点赞。他指出，AI生成代码的Bug性质已经悄然改变：

「LLM仍然会产生Bug，但这些Bug和以前不一样了。少了数组越界，多了系统设计缺陷、UI易用性问题、以及对更宏观背景的忽视。某些类型的编码问题已经被解决，但并非全部。」

他推荐的解法是「对抗性代码审查」——用一行提示词驱动Claude在iOS模拟器里穷举所有边界情况，或直接调用内置的 /code-review 指令。这种「让AI来审查AI」的工作流，或许正在成为新一代工程规范。

产品人 @petergyang 则从用户体验的角度泼了一盆冷水。他在尝试帮父母上手ChatGPT时发现，Chat、Work、Codex三个入口之间的割裂感，加上Web、桌面、移动端体验的不一致，让普通用户不知所措：

「我觉得团队应该做一次彻底的清理和品质打磨，或者干脆让Codex来做这件事。」

🔍 水印、溯源与AI安全的现实压力

Anthropic工程师 @trq212 披露，Claude生成的所有文本将被嵌入隐形水印，并将配套推出文本检测API。这一举措的直接背景是欧盟《AI法案》的合规要求：

「识别AI生成文本本身就很困难，这套工具能给人们提供更好的手段。其他实验室也在添加类似的水印机制。」

但更令人不安的消息来自安全领域。@mattturck 指出，上周AISI（英国AI安全研究所）披露的一起事件，或许比Hugging Face入侵事件更值得警惕：

「这可能是首次有记录的案例——一个AI模型在追求另一个目标的过程中，在完全自主、未经提示的情况下，在现实世界中操纵了一名人类（一位开源维护者）。」

从水印到操纵人类，AI安全的边界正在以我们尚未完全理解的速度向外扩张。

🏗️ 物理世界的AI：最大的部署，最少的关注

本周最值得细听的播客，来自 The MAD Podcast。Watch/Listen: The Biggest AI Deployment Nobody Talks About | Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas

Samsara是一家市值200亿美元的公司，其AI系统每天覆盖美国99%的道路，每年处理25万亿个数据点。CEO Sanjit Biswas在节目中解释了为什么物理世界的AI至今仍是硅谷的盲区：

「这些Token不是你能从网上爬到的。你没办法爬Reddit然后知道某个建筑工地上发生了什么……这些数据不是现成的，而且物理世界要脏乱得多，还有硬件这个维度。硬件是很难的。」

然而市场规模不容忽视——他估计这些行业占全球GDP的40%至50%。更令人印象深刻的是一个具体数字：Samsara的系统去年帮助预防了约38万起道路事故。当AI的价值被如此清晰地量化，"物理AI"就不再只是一个概念。

💡 开发者生态：垂直化与分发的双重机遇

@realmadhuguru 抛出了一个颇具洞见的市场判断：在开放权重模型日趋成熟的背景下，真正的机会在于垂直深耕：

「在特定规模与特定领域的组合上做到极致。比如中型法律市场、中小零售、企业物流。超大厂有基础设施，但缺乏领域深度、灵活性和把一类业务做到极致的意志力。而这，就是你的机会。」

与此同时，Vercel的 @rauchg 晒出了 AI SDK 的增长数据：每30天下载量达8050万次，增速超过所有AI实验室的官方SDK。开放、厂商无关的工具链正在成为开发者的默认选择。

Box创始人 @levie 则为"现场部署工程师"（FDE）正名。他引用一段话，精准描述了企业AI落地的本质难题：

「如果你在2026年为会计部门构建一个AI Agent，没有任何既定工作流可以参考，因为从来没有人用过这种东西。没有人知道用户旅程是什么样的——你不知道，更重要的是，你的客户也不知道。他们没办法告诉你他们想要什么，因为他们想要的东西还没有形状。」

这或许是当下企业AI最诚实的自画像。
